title: R. v. Reyes & Cole — Counterfeit Watches (pinned-persona A/B)
charge_or_claim: Fraud over $5,000 (Criminal Code s.380) — the Crown alleges the two accused sold counterfeit 'luxury' watches as genuine, taking about $30,000 from buyers who were told the watches were authentic and carried a manufacturer warranty.
_AB_NOTE: Flip the two pinned personas below (swap their styles, or make the Crown meek and the Defence fierce) and re-run to see how advocacy STYLE alone moves the same jury on the same facts. Judge + witnesses stay auto-cast.

crown_persona.name: Vincent Hale, KC
crown_persona.background: a feared senior Crown with a reputation for theatrical jury addresses
crown_persona.style: aggressive and relentless; hammers the jury with rhetorical questions, presses every inference hard, and treats any doubt as an excuse

defense_persona.name: Maggie Ellsworth
defense_persona.background: a beloved small-town defence lawyer who has never lost a jury's trust
defense_persona.style: warm, folksy and plain-spoken; slows everything down, talks to the jury like neighbours, and gently keeps returning to reasonable doubt

defendants.name: Mateo Reyes
defendants.account: I sold the watches my supplier gave me and repeated what he told me — that they were authentic. I never inspected paperwork and had no idea they might be fakes.

defendants.name: Dana Cole
defendants.account: I sourced the watches from a wholesaler whose documentation said they were genuine. I believed they were authentic and passed on the same papers I received.

witnesses.name: Priya Nair
witnesses.what_they_know: I paid $6,000 for a watch Mateo Reyes told me was a genuine Swiss luxury model with a manufacturer warranty. A jeweller later told me it was a counterfeit worth about $40.

witnesses.name: Sam Whitfield
witnesses.what_they_know: I am a watch appraiser. These counterfeits are high quality and the accompanying paperwork looks authentic; an ordinary seller could plausibly believe they were genuine.

your_side: The defence says neither accused knew the watches were counterfeit. Fraud requires dishonest intent, and the Crown cannot prove either accused knew the goods were fake — they relied in good faith on their suppliers and on documentation that appeared genuine.
